exam.title: Object-Oriented System Analysis and Design (OOSAD)
exam.instructions: This exam covers object-oriented programming principles, Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) methodologies, the Unified Process, and the Unified Modeling Language (UML). Answer all questions carefully. Answers are provided at the end.

questions.text: Which list correctly identifies the essential elements of the Object Model, as opposed to useful but non-essential elements?

options.text: Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism
Abstraction, Encapsulation, Modularity, Hierarchy
Abstraction, Modularity, Typing, Concurrency
Encapsulation, Modularity, Persistence, Concurrency
Hierarchy, Typing, Concurrency, Persistence

questions.text: What is the fundamental difference in focus between Abstraction and Encapsulation in object-oriented programming?

options.text: Abstraction hides implementation details, while encapsulation focuses on essential characteristics.
Abstraction classifies phenomena into concepts, while encapsulation focuses on data manipulation procedures.
Abstraction extracts essential characteristics distinguishing an object, whereas encapsulation focuses on the implementation that gives rise to the object's observable behavior.
Abstraction deals with observable behavior, whereas encapsulation modularizes system features into classes and methods.
Abstraction represents abstract actors, while encapsulation packages unrelated operations.

questions.text: For a project with significant architectural risks and a government sponsor focused on risk management, which SDLC model is best suited due to its risk management focus, despite its complexity?

options.text: Waterfall Model
Rapid Application Development (RAD)
Prototyping Model
Spiral Model
Incremental & Iterative Approach

questions.text: How does Aggregation differ from Association, and what type of relationship does Aggregation represent?

options.text: Aggregation is a relationship where one class uses another, represented as a binary relationship.
Aggregation is a collection of things, represented by a 'has a' relationship, indicating a whole-to-part structure.
Aggregation describes a set of links, representing a connection among objects.
Aggregation denotes cardinality ratios in a binary association.
Aggregation is a semantic relationship where a change in one element affects another.

questions.text: Which example best illustrates operator overloading within polymorphism?

options.text: A function name handling different numbers and types of arguments, like a word with multiple meanings.
A Person superclass with subclasses (Doctor, Mechanic, Cook) where the 'Work' message varies by subclass.
The addition operation producing a sum for numbers but concatenating strings into a third string.
Objects with different internal structures sharing the same external interface for uniform access.
Objects taking multiple forms, derived from a Greek term meaning multiple forms.

questions.text: In the Incremental & Iterative Approach, what is the primary function of the Control List?

options.text: A static list of required features for the first release.
A dynamic list specifying design changes and new requirements based on user interaction and analysis.
A detailed list of steps in a use case’s normal flow with discrete sub-steps.
A prioritized list of use cases based on risk, addressing critical ones first.
A list of defects from the previous version to be corrected before adding new requirements.

sections.title: Matching Questions
sections.instructions: Match each term or concept from List A with its most fitting description or characteristic from List B.

listB.text: A modular unit with independent deployment and specified interface(s).
An executable procedure in a class, invoked via message passing.
Reducing something to essential characteristics distinguishing an object.
An object’s property of transcending time and/or space.
Compartmentalizing an abstraction, hiding inner workings.
A system decomposed into cohesive, loosely coupled modules.
A data element in a record or variable.
Building objects from other objects, enabling property acquisition.
A role interacting with the system.
A collection of methods and attributes defining behaviors.

shortAnswer.answer: Polymorphism, from Greek 'many forms,' allows objects to be treated uniformly despite different behaviors. Operator overloading redefines operators (e.g., '+' for numbers vs. strings), while function overloading uses the same function name with different parameters. It enables shared external interfaces via common methods and supports inheritance by allowing subclasses to override parent behaviors.

Unified Process principles: (1) Use case driven: Development is guided by use cases defining system functionality. (2) Architecture centered: Focus on a robust system structure early. (3) Iterative and incremental: Build in cycles, refining the system. (4) Risk oriented: Prioritize addressing high-risk elements to ensure project success.

Association is a structural UML relationship representing connections among objects (e.g., 'Student enrolls in Course'). Aggregation is a 'has a' whole-to-part relationship, a special association where parts can exist independently (e.g., 'Car has a Wheel'). Aggregation implies a weaker dependency compared to Association.

Use Case Scenario steps: (1) Normal Flow: Main success path (mandatory). (2) Alternate Flow: Variations from normal path. (3) Sub-Flows: Reusable sub-steps. (4) Exceptions: Error conditions. Only Normal Flow is mandatory, defining the primary interaction sequence.

Activity Diagrams focus on workflow, showing dynamic process flows with nodes and edges (e.g., use case steps). Sequence Diagrams emphasize interaction timing, depicting messages between objects along a vertical timeline. Activity Diagrams model processes; Sequence Diagrams model object interactions.
